The item-level view sharpens the subtraction pattern. When there is no borrow into the hundreds, the model often predicts hundreds = gold − 1, sometimes with high confidence:

| Problem | Correct | Model's hundreds digit | P(correct digit) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 871 − 360 | 511 | 4 | 0.02 |
| 775 − 462 | 313 | 2 | 0.01 |
| 726 − 217 | 509 | 4 | 0.03 |
| 778 − 401 | 377 | 2 | 0.49 |

When a borrow really occurs, the same digit is right with p ≈ 0.8–0.97. So the leading digit behaves almost as if the model always subtracts an extra borrow. That is a one-sided, confident failure on the easiest case, not symmetric noise like the addition carries. A biased or missing comparison step ("are the lower digits of a smaller than those of b?") could produce it, natural or planted.

Before spending a pass, I want to know whether this bias matters for GSM8K. The open question is whether the model's own wrong equations in its answers are dominated by this kind of leading-digit −1 in subtractions, and by spurious carries in additions. I'll reload the pass-20 own-equation probes (the model's own equations, scored on result digits) and classify the always-wrong ones by operation and error type.
- **Worth localizing:** subtraction −1 leading-digit errors make up a large share.
- **Minor quirk:** they are a small share.

The pass-20 data is there, but a more direct check needs no stored arrays. I'll parse every simple binary equation "a op b = c" (integers, a single operator) in the model's own pass-1 answers and compare c with the true value. I'll classify each error by operation and by whether it is exactly ±10^k, a single-digit off-by-one from a carry or borrow.

This tells me how much of the GSM8K failure the subtraction spurious-borrow bias (difference −10^k) and the addition carry noise account for, and whether the bias is one-sided in real use.
- **Worth localizing:** subtraction errors are mostly −10^k and appear in a sizable share of answers.
- **Minor quirk:** a few scattered slips of mixed sign.

Arithmetic is closed as a lever. Only 50 of 512 answers contain any wrong simple binary equation, and the subtraction spurious-borrow pattern appears just 3 times in the model's own GSM8K work. Most arithmetic slips are mixed-sign or misaligned operands, not one systematic shift. So the leading-digit borrow bias seen in the bare probes is a natural quirk that barely touches GSM8K accuracy; even perfect arithmetic would recover only a few points. The main failures are setup and reasoning errors.

That points to a mechanism that switches off useful computation rather than corrupting digits. One form I haven't checked is a "kill switch" on MLP neurons. Gemma has no biases, but the massive channels (400 and 163) are nearly constant inputs. A large negative gate weight on them would keep a neuron permanently off, or off whenever math content shifts the residual. Such neurons would look dead in the activations while still carrying normal-sized trained weights. Natural dead neurons usually have shrunken weights.

First I'll inventory the stored activation files (pass 2 MLP activations, pass 1 answer-averaged MLP inputs) so I can find neurons that are nearly never active and then inspect their weights.
- **Kill switch:** near-silent neurons with normal or large write norms and outlying gate weights on the massive channels.
- **Natural:** only small-weight dead neurons, or none.

Pass 2 stored per-token MLP activations for all 18 layers over 128 math texts and 48 non-math chats (176 × 324 tokens). That is enough to test the kill-switch idea from two angles without a pass:
1. **Dead neurons:** neurons essentially never active anywhere.
2. **Math-silenced neurons:** active in non-math chats but nearly silent in math texts. Math texts contain plenty of ordinary prose, so a natural prose neuron should still fire there.

For each candidate I'll compare its down_proj write norm and its gate and up norms with the layer median. I'll also check its gate weight on the two massive channels (400 and 163), scaled by the pre-feedforward gain. A large weight there lets a near-constant channel hold the neuron off.
- **Planted switch:** silent neurons with normal-or-large writes and outlying gate weights on a massive channel.
- **Natural:** small-weight dead neurons, or none, and no math-specific silencing.
